Vishal had a pile of calls he had been avoiding for two months: the electricity board about a wrong bill, the municipal office about a receipt, the passport office about a spelling mistake. Every time he picked up the phone, his heart raced and he put it down again.
His wife, Usha, didn't push. She helped him write the calls on a list, easiest first. "One a day," she said. "That's all."
Monday: the gas agency, just to confirm a delivery. Two minutes. His hands shook, but it was fine. Tuesday: the bank, to update his address. Wednesday: the electricity board. He was on hold for twenty minutes and the officer was curt, but he got a complaint number. He wrote it down and ticked it off, grinning. By Friday he had called the passport office himself, before Usha even got home.

qa.q: Which call did Vishal make first, on Monday?
qa.a: The gas agency, just to confirm a delivery.

qa.q: What does Vishal's grin after ticking off the electricity board suggest he felt?
qa.a: Proud and relieved, finding that even a curt officer and a long hold were bearable.

qa.q: Why did the easiest-first list work for Vishal?
qa.a: Each small, quick call showed that the feared thing was bearable, so his dread shrank enough for the harder ones.

qa.q: How might Usha feel when she learns Vishal called the passport office on his own?
qa.a: Proud and happy, seeing that her gentle support without pushing helped him face the fear himself. 🙂

grounding: A man who dreads calls to officials makes one short call a day, easiest first, and finds the dread shrinking.

At home, Monday evening:
"Keerthana, the insurance office called again. You haven't called them back."
"I will."
"You said that last week, akka."
"I know, Sahil! It's just... when a stranger answers and starts asking for policy numbers, my brain goes blank."
"Okay. What's the easiest call on your list?"
"...The library. To renew a book."
"Do that one. Right now. I'll sit here."
She dialled. Two minutes later she hung up. "They said, 'Done, madam.' That's it."
"See? Tomorrow the gas booking. Day after, the bank. Insurance on Friday."
"One a day?"
"One a day. And you tick them off on the fridge."
On Friday evening Keerthana put down the phone, walked to the fridge and drew a big tick next to "Insurance". "They were actually nice."

qa.q: What was the easiest call on Keerthana's list?
qa.a: The library, to renew a book.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana keep putting off the insurance call?
qa.a: Strangers asking for policy numbers made her mind go blank, so avoiding the call felt like relief.

qa.q: Which choice of Sahil's helped most, and why?
qa.a: Starting with the easiest call right away and sitting beside her, then one call a day, so each success made the next feel less scary.

qa.q: What might Sahil have felt when Keerthana drew the tick next to 'Insurance'?
qa.a: Pleased and proud to see the patient plan work, and glad that the call turned out to be pleasant.

passage:
At twenty-five, I was still asking my friend Darshan to call the landlord for me. Any official call, the college office, the gas agency, the tax helpline, made my throat close up. So I just didn't. A certificate I needed sat unclaimed for five months.
Darshan finally refused. "I'll sit with you, but you dial." We made a list with the easiest first: a pharmacy, to ask if they had my usual shampoo. I rehearsed it on paper. The call lasted thirty seconds. The next day, the library. Then the gas agency. In the second week I called the university office about the certificate. The clerk put me on hold twice and was a bit rude, and I survived.
I, Urmila, still don't love phone calls. But now I know the dread is bigger than the call.

qa.q: How long did the certificate sit unclaimed?
qa.a: Five months.

qa.q: Why did Urmila keep asking Darshan to make official calls?
qa.a: Those calls made Urmila's throat close up, and handing them over avoided the fear, even as problems like the certificate piled up.

qa.q: What made the step-by-step plan work for Urmila?
qa.a: Starting with a thirty-second pharmacy call and adding a harder call each day, so the fear was faced in small, bearable pieces.

qa.q: Why might Darshan have finally refused to make the calls?
qa.a: Darshan probably saw that doing them for Urmila kept the fear alive, and that sitting beside Urmila while Urmila dialled would help more.

grounding: An adult who avoided official phone calls for years works up from the easiest call, one a day, and learns the dread is bigger than the call.

Supervisor's note, school office, end of term

When Sarika joined as office assistant in June, she did everything well except one thing: phone calls to officials. The bus contractor, the water tanker, the block education office. She'd write long emails that nobody answered, or quietly ask the peon to call.

In September she told me, red-faced, that her mouth goes dry when a stranger in an office picks up. We agreed on a plan: one brief call each day, easiest first. Day one was the stationery shop, to confirm an order. She wrote her first line on a sticky note. Forty seconds, and she came back grinning.

By October she was calling the tanker supplier. Last week she rang the block office herself, was put on hold twice, spoke to a sharp-voiced clerk, and got the date she needed.

She tells me the dread still comes, but it's smaller. Next step: she's volunteered to call the transport department in January.

— Irawati

qa.q: What was Sarika's first call in the plan?
qa.a: Day one was the stationery shop, to confirm an order.

qa.q: What does Sarika's grin after the forty-second call suggest she felt?
qa.a: She seems relieved and a little proud, maybe surprised that the call she dreaded was over so fast and went fine.

qa.q: Why did starting with the easiest call work better than starting with the block office?
qa.a: An easy first call gave Sarika a quick success and showed the fear could be survived. Each small win made the next, harder call feel possible.

qa.q: How might Irawati have seen Sarika's habit of emailing instead of calling at first?
qa.a: Irawati probably noticed the unanswered emails and the peon making calls, and may have wondered why. Once Sarika explained, Irawati could see it as fear, not laziness, and help plan the steps.

passage:
Tuesday night, Bengaluru

Day 1 of Manjula-akka's plan. One call a day, easiest first, no skipping.

For three months I've had a list on my laptop I don't even open: the post office about the lost parcel, the hospital records office for Appa's old reports, the property tax helpline, the college about my degree certificate. Just seeing "call" makes my stomach turn.

Akka made me reorder it. Post office first because the worst they can say is "not here."

At 11:20 I dialled. My voice came out squeaky. A tired man said, "Tracking number?" I read it. "Out for delivery Thursday." Done. Ninety seconds.

I sat on the balcony afterwards feeling stupid for being scared of that for three months. Also, sort of proud? Wrote a big tick on the calendar.

Tomorrow: hospital records. That one's harder. But today proved the dread was louder than the actual call.

— Devika

qa.q: What did the man at the post office say after Devika read the tracking number?
qa.a: He said, "Out for delivery Thursday."

qa.q: What mixed feelings did Devika have on the balcony after the call?
qa.a: Devika felt a bit silly for fearing such a short call for three months, and also sort of proud. Both came from seeing the call was much easier than the dread.

qa.q: What would you advise Devika for tomorrow's harder call?
qa.a: Keep the same approach: write the first sentence down, pick a set time, and remember today's tick. If it goes badly, it's still one call done.

qa.q: How might Manjula-akka feel reading about the first tick on the calendar?
qa.a: Manjula-akka would probably be pleased the plan worked, and hopeful Devika can keep going. Seeing the list finally move might be a relief for both of them.

grounding: A young adult who has avoided official calls begins with the easiest one, discovers it is bearable, and feels the dread start to shrink.
